title: Self-Describing Threshold
statement:
You get an array nums of non-negative integers. Find an integer x such that exactly x elements of nums are greater than or equal to x.

x does not have to be one of the values in nums. If such an x exists it is unique; return it. Otherwise return -1.

examples.why: Three values (3, 5 and 4) are at least 3.
Both values are at least 2. The answer 2 does not appear in the array.
x = 1 counts 3 values, x = 2 counts 1, x = 0 counts 3 and x = 3 counts 0. None match.

hints: The answer, if it exists, is between 0 and n: you can never have more than n elements at least x.
As x grows, the number of elements ≥ x can only shrink. One side rises, the other falls, so they meet at most once.
Sort the array. For a candidate x, the count of elements ≥ x is n minus the position of the first element ≥ x, which binary search finds. Or count values into buckets 0..n and sweep from the top.

explain.intuition:
Let count(x) be the number of elements at least x. Only x from 0 to n can work, because count(x) is never more than n. As x increases, count(x) never increases. A rising line and a falling staircase can cross at most once, which is why the answer is unique.

After sorting, count(x) is n − (index of the first element ≥ x), a binary search. You can also binary search on x itself: if count(x) > x, the answer must be larger; if count(x) < x, it must be smaller. For an O(n) version, cap every value at n, count how many land in each bucket, and sweep x from n down while keeping a running total of elements ≥ x.
steps: For the middle x, find the first index i with nums[i] ≥ x (another binary search); then count = n − i.
If count === x, return x. If count > x, search higher; otherwise search lower.
pitfalls: Trying only the values that appear in the array. In [7, 8] the answer is 2.
Using greater than instead of greater than or equal when counting.
Not testing x = n or x = 0, the two ends of the range.

solutions.title: Try every x
solutions.idea: For each x from 0 to n, count the elements at least x.

solutions.title: Sort, then binary search on x
solutions.idea: count(x) falls as x rises. Compare count(x) with x to decide which half holds the answer.

solutions.title: Counting buckets
solutions.idea: Values above n behave like n. Bucket them, then sweep x downward with a running count of elements ≥ x.

followups: This is the idea behind a researcher's h-index. How does that definition differ, and why can it always be computed?
The array arrives already sorted. Can you answer in O(log n)?
